sections.title: The Lowdown
sections.content_md:
Your teams are like newborn babies at this point - full of potential, can do no wrong, and just require a bit of care and feeding to not completely die. They haven't started school, haven't gotten arrested or pregnant, and every single one of them could grow up to be a doctor, lawyer, astronaut, and/or multi-millionaire. Some of your teams (the one with Josh Jacobs, for example - Bandit before he dropped him)  were born with birth defects, but he's been to GE26 and is used to suffering, and probably is still springing with hope eternal (like our many Bears fans) to reach escape velocity with an aide job. Anyway, best of luck everyone!

This league page was built using ChatGPT paired with Claude Code, which pushes to GitHub and then to Vercel to host the page. While some of the tabs are populated with AI-generated content, and I use AI to help research each section, the Lowdown and the matchups will always be typed up by yours-truly. A newsletter with no soul doesn't rate a read as far as I'm concerned.

Come back with any BGCs!

sections.title: Common Tactical Picture
sections.content_md:
### Wild SeeKats (Seebass/Kats) vs Los Bandidos (Bandit)

I regret giving the SeeKats my exact draft rankings, unedited - many snipes occurred. The combined logistics expertise of Kats combined with Seebass' killer instinct to yield truly scary offspring. Wild SeeKats is one of two two-parent households in the league, and it shows in the tidiest team in the nursery: Jahmyr Gibbs and Breece Hall, A.J. Brown and George Pickens, and Jayden Daniels under center (if he can stay healthy). There's a second tight end jammed into the FLEX, because Harold Fannin was the healthiest kid in the crib. Single parent Bandit is raising Trey McBride and George Kittle in one house with a single tight end slot between them - two cribs and one bedroom. He also surgically corrected the birth defect in his team and dropped Josh Jacobs. Two parents and one lineup against one parent and one too many tight ends.

### Statistical Anomalies (McLovin) vs L’entente Discordiale (Borat/Jack)

Borat (and Jack, for like three picks) showed up with a beautiful full-term baby: Christian McCaffrey in year ten, Josh Allen, Ashton Jeanty, and Mike Evans (year 13!) riding the bench next to DK Metcalf and a second team defense nobody needs. They may have designed a better infant team. Then, see my team:  one of the preemies of the litter: Jeremiyah Love and TreVeyon Henderson in the backfield, Carnell Tate and De'Zhaun Stribling on the bench, and Juwan Johnson at tight end, who is less a starter than a responsible adult I asked to babysit the rest of the team. Statistical anomalies will be required for my hopium team to triumph here.

### SHACtin' a Fool 🐻 (SHAC) vs Dave

SHAC is a Weapons Director by trade. His literal job is looking at a picture, listening to comms, and noticing what's missing; he took a similar approach to team construction. He drafted Lamar Jackson, Bijan Robinson, Malik Nabers and Kyle Pitts, then took two defenses (poor WRM), then took no kicker whatsoever. To this day (Friday the 4th) his K slot remains as empty as our concepts backlog, and he remains the only team without a complete set of limbs/internal organs/chromosomes - pick your metaphor. Dave (or rather, his McLovin/SHAC-aligned militia group, since he was executing a water birth) similarly missed a position (DST) but stacked depth: Xavier Worthy, Marvin Harrison and Stefon Diggs are sitting on his bench behind CeeDee Lamb and Brock Bowers. Overall, a very defensible lineup, other than the fact he dropped an 11th-round pick to grab a DST.

### MJS HURT Locker (MJ) vs Swifty Mahomey (Pappie)

Grandpappie drafted a team that almost averages 30 years old (29.2). His infant team entered the world with a monk haircut and strong opinions about "the good old times" and gardening. Pappie is starting Travis Kelce in his 14th season and Davante Adams in his 13th, with Matthew Stafford (18th) parked on the bench in case of (extreme, hopefully-avoidable) emergency. MJ is leading a similarly ancient baby (?) team headlined by Derrick Henry in year 11 and Aaron Jones in year 10 (same draft class as Myles Garrett, Trubisky, Fournette, CMC, Mixon, James Conner, old D-Watson, and finally Mahomes, who ended up on Pappie's team). Both had the sense to put a real receiver out front, Justin Jefferson on one side and Amon-Ra St. Brown on the other, which is the only reason either baby daycare passes inspection. Someone go get these two teams some butterscotch candies and rocking chairs.

### Swanson vs Gary

The other baby with no kicker at the draft, ol' Jesse (Ron?) Swanson, has Puka, Rashee Rice and Chase Brown - altogether a healthy infant team with unusually good hands but tiny legs; he fixed the empty K slot by kicking 15th-round pick Alvin Kamara to the curb so Jesse could loop in Tyler. On the other hand, Gary assembled one of the most aggressively healthy, coordinated, and vocal rosters in the league: Herbert, Jonathan Taylor, Kyren Williams, DeVonta Smith, Ladd, and Tucker Kraft. Nothing wrong with any of it, unless Tucker is slow to come back from last year's injury. Definitely nothing that would put either team in the NICU, and they're probably both good to take their teams home from the hospital the next morning.

sections.title: Custom Section
sections.content_md:
**What's in a Name? City Fantasy Team Build**

The premise: build the best fantasy starting lineup in which every player's own first or last name is exactly the name of a real city. One QB, two RB, two WR, one TE, one K. Exact matches only, so no nicknames and no partial credit for living inside a longer name.

The rule that decides everything is municipal class rather than size. The place has to be a city, which means a town, a village or a borough gets you nothing no matter how many people live there.

QB Josh Allen (BUF) — Allen, Texas · 104,627
RB Bijan Robinson (ATL) — Robinson, Illinois · 7,150
RB Jonathan Taylor (IND) — Taylor, Michigan · 63,409
WR Ja'Marr Chase (CIN) — Chase, Kansas · 396
WR Justin Jefferson (MIN) — Jefferson, Georgia · 13,233
TE Colston Loveland (CHI) — Loveland, Colorado · 76,378
K Brandon Aubrey (DAL) — Aubrey, Texas · 5,006

That is the consensus 2nd, 3rd, 8th, 11th and 27th players off the board, plus TE3 and the best kicker in football. I went looking for seven names that technically worked and came back with a first-round board that happens to carry a residency requirement. Chase, Kansas has 396 people in it and is carrying the WR1.

**OUTSIDE CITY LIMITS**

Three of the best players in football exist as municipalities, not cities:

Jahmyr Gibbs — the consensus number one overall player in fantasy football. Gibbs, Missouri is a village of 70.
Brock Bowers — TE1. Bowers, Delaware is a town of 278. Chase, Kansas is a city of 396.
Trey McBride — TE2. McBride, Michigan is a village of 189.
Amon-Ra St. Brown — his surname is St. Brown, and there is no St. Brown town.

**THE ALL-MARQUEE TEAM**

Then somebody is going to point out that Chase, Kansas is not a proper city, so here is the same exercise with one extra rule: the city needs at least 100,000 residents.

This rule costs the roster the consensus RB1, RB2, WR1, TE3 and K1, and only one man survives from the first team.

QB Josh Allen (BUF) — Allen, Texas · 104,627
RB Omarion Hampton (LAC) — Hampton, Virginia · 137,148
RB Bucky Irving (TB) — Irving, Texas · 256,684
WR Drake London (ATL) — London, England · 9,089,736
WR Parker Washington (JAX) — Washington, D.C. · 689,545
TE Tyler Warren (IND) — Warren, Michigan · 139,387
K Tyler Loop (BAL) — Tyler, Texas · 105,995

London means the one in England, because London, Ohio is 10,279 people and fails the floor. Washington is here on a written exception: the Census Bureau's own District of Columbia guide says the District has one city, its population glossary says the District is a county, and I picked the reading that got me a receiver.

And the kicker slot is the whole bit in one line. The entire qualifying pool in the National Football League is two men, and they are both Tylers (Loop and Bass).

Close, but no cigar: Lawrence, Kansas has 94,934 residents. Trevor Lawrence needed 5,066 more Jayhawks - not that he was going to beat Allen anyway.

sections.title: Peer and Near-Peer Competition
sections.content_md:
1. **Los Bandidos (Bandit)** · Peer Competition — The cleanest starting lineup in the league: Saquon Barkley and De'Von Achane at RB, Drake London/Tee Higgins/Terry McLaurin at WR, and the absurd luxury of Trey McBride and George Kittle. Depth is thinner than the stars suggest, but nobody wants to play the first seven names on this roster.
2. **L’entente Discordiale (Borat/Jack)** · Peer Competition — Josh Allen plus Christian McCaffrey and Ashton Jeanty gives the coalition an elite weekly spine before Nico Collins, Garrett Wilson, DK Metcalf and Mike Evans even enter the discussion. The automated board is much colder on this team than I am; starter quality matters more here than the depth-weighted room rankings.
3. **Wild SeeKats (Seebass/Kats)** · Peer Competition — Jahmyr Gibbs enters Week 1 as the consensus RB1, Jayden Daniels remains an elite QB, and Breece Hall gives the backfield a second hammer. The WR room is shallower than the contenders above them, but the ceiling at QB/RB is enough to make this a legitimate title roster.
4. **SHACtin' a Fool 🐻 (SHAC)** · Near-Peer Competition — Lamar Jackson and Bijan Robinson provide two players capable of winning a week by themselves, with Malik Nabers, Jaylen Waddle and Kyle Pitts supplying plenty behind them. The RB depth gets questionable quickly after Bijan/Omarion Hampton, so the margin for injury is smaller than the star power suggests.
5. **MJS HURT Locker (MJ)** · Near-Peer Competition — Jalen Hurts, Derrick Henry, Bucky Irving, Amon-Ra St. Brown and the LaPorta/Andrews TE pair are much stronger than a last-place automated model-board ranking implies. This roster has fewer obvious holes than several teams above it; the question is whether the aging pieces around the core remain useful enough.
6. **Dave** · Near-Peer Competition — CeeDee Lamb, James Cook, Brock Bowers and Zay Flowers give Dave a legitimate weekly foundation, with Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jameson Williams adding ceiling. Dak Prescott is not an advantage at QB, but in a 1QB league that weakness matters considerably less than it would in Disco.
7. **Swifty Mahomey (Pappie)** · Near-Peer Competition — Patrick Mahomes, Justin Jefferson and Jaxon Smith-Njigba are a strong nucleus, and David Montgomery gives the RB room a useful Week 1 matchup. The concern is age and volatility elsewhere: Kelce, Davante Adams, Deebo Samuel and the secondary backs leave more ways for the roster to decay than the teams above it.
8. **Statistical Anomalies (McLovin)** · Competitive but Flawed — Joe Burrow throwing to a roster headlined by Ja'Marr Chase, Brian Thomas Jr. and Chris Olave gives this team plenty of weekly ceiling. The TE room is a real disadvantage and the backfield arrives with more injury/role uncertainty than I want from a contender, including Jeremiyah Love's ankle situation.
9. **Gary** · Competitive but Flawed — Jonathan Taylor and Kyren Williams are a strong RB pairing and Justin Herbert gets a favorable Week 1 setup, but the roster loses ground against this league's elite teams at WR and TE. There is enough balance to beat anyone; there are fewer positional mismatches working in Gary's favor.
10. **Swanson** · Competitive but Flawed — Puka Nacua and Rashee Rice can carry a lot of weight, and Chase Brown gives the backfield a credible lead option. After that, too much depends on Caleb Williams taking another step and younger pieces like Colston Loveland and Luther Burden developing quickly; the floor is lower than the other nine rosters.

sections.title: Tracks of Interest
sections.content_md: Justin Herbert, QB — Gary — LAC vs. ARI There are easier ways to begin a fantasy season than asking Justin Herbert to throw against a secondary that finished 24th in passing yards allowed. RotoBaller has Herbert as a strong QB1 and points to the combination of Mike McDaniel taking over the offense and a healthy offensive line as reasons to expect another step forward. FantasyPros' current Week 1 Superflex consensus has Herbert all the way up at QB5, while FanDuel notes Arizona surrendered 230.8 passing yards per game last season. This isn't a streamer getting promoted by matchup; it's a good quarterback entering Week 1 with both the offensive environment and opponent pushing in the same direction. The play: Strong QB1. Arizona provides a good first test of whether the McDaniel-Herbert pairing is going to produce the fantasy jump everyone spent August pricing in. Bucky Irving, RB — MJ — TB at CIN Cincinnati's 2025 run defense was less a defensive unit than an invitation. FanDuel has the Bengals dead last in rushing defense at 147.1 yards allowed per game, while RotoBaller notes they surrendered the most fantasy points and rushing yards to opposing backs. That outlet calls Irving a strong RB2 even with Kenny Gainwell around, and FantasyPros experts overwhelmingly preferred Irving in a current Week 1 comparison against Christian Watson. Tampa Bay does not need to invent volume here. The opponent should give Irving enough opportunity on its own. The play: RB2 with legitimate upside. If Cincinnati's front looks anything like last year's version, Irving could spend a lot of Sunday making the offseason timeshare discussion feel unnecessarily complicated. Kyle Pitts, TE — SHACtin' a Fool 🐻 (SHAC) — ATL at PIT This would normally be the point where everyone remembers the previous four years of Kyle Pitts discourse and reaches for the eject handle. The difference this time is that the breakout already happened. Pitts finished 2025 as the PPR TE2 with career highs in receptions and touchdowns, and Pittsburgh allowed the second-most fantasy points to opposing tight ends. FantasyPros currently has him TE5 for Week 1, while FanDuel notes the Steelers finished 29th in pass defense overall. The player, role and matchup are all finally telling the same story. The play: Clear TE1. This is the rare Kyle Pitts recommendation based on what he has already done rather than what we have spent years hoping he might eventually do. David Montgomery, RB — Swifty Mahomey (PAPPIE) — HOU vs. BUF Montgomery gets one of the cleanest Week 1 volume/matchup combinations outside the elite tier. Buffalo finished 28th in rushing defense at 136.2 yards allowed per game, and RotoBaller specifically identifies Montgomery as a Week 1 matchup it loves after the Bills surrendered the sixth-most fantasy points to running backs in 2025. FantasyPros has him around RB20 in half-PPR, which is useful context: this is not an obvious top-five start, but rather a player whose weekly circumstances look better than the generic ranking. Houston may rotate Woody Marks, but Montgomery is expected to lead the backfield. The play: Strong RB2. Buffalo's run defense gives Montgomery a realistic route to beating the fairly modest consensus ranking. Jayden Daniels, QB — Wild SeeKats (Seebass/Kats) — WAS at PHI Philadelphia is a good defense, which is exactly why Daniels is interesting here. The Eagles finished eighth against the pass, and FanDuel's projection is relatively restrained at 15.5 fantasy points. The counter is the one matchup trait that matters enormously for Daniels: Philadelphia allowed the second-most quarterback rushing yards and rushing touchdowns last season. RotoBaller still grades him as a solid QB1, while FantasyPros has him QB6 in its Week 1 Superflex consensus. A difficult conventional quarterback matchup becomes considerably less conventional when the quarterback is part running back. The play: QB1. The passing matchup may suppress his ceiling somewhat, but Philadelphia's 2025 vulnerability to mobile quarterbacks gives Daniels a very different escape route.

sections.title: Fades
sections.content_md: DK Metcalf, WR — L'entente Discordiale (Borat/Jack) — PIT vs. ATL Metcalf is expected to play after entering Week 1 with an injury issue, but "available" and "good fantasy setup" are different questions. RotoBaller expects possible shadow coverage from A.J. Terrell and drops Metcalf to lower-end WR3 territory. FanDuel projects just 49.5 receiving yards and 9.4 PPR points. FantasyPros is somewhat more optimistic and calls him a strong FLEX now that his health has cleared, so this is not a unanimous bench call. It is a warning against treating the name on the roster as an automatic WR2. The fade: FLEX, not set-and-forget WR2. The combination of recent injury and Terrell makes the downside considerably more credible than Metcalf's name value suggests. Jeremiyah Love, RB — Statistical Anomalies (McLovin) — ARI at LAC There are several independent ways this goes wrong. Love is coming back from a preseason high-ankle sprain, FantasyPros reported him as roughly 50/50 for Week 1 earlier this week, and even if active he gets a Chargers defense that allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points to running backs last season. RotoBaller still sees RB2 value if he suits up, but explicitly recommends tempering expectations in his NFL debut. FantasyPros' own Derek Brown is below consensus because the ankle clouds both availability and early-season effectiveness. That's enough compounding uncertainty to avoid betting aggressively on his first professional game. The fade: Sit if there is a credible alternative. If he is active, he is still playable, but "rookie debut + high ankle sprain + top-tier RB defense" is an impressive collection of reasons to make someone else prove it first. Rashee Rice, WR — Swanson — KC vs. DEN Rice is probably still going into many lineups, but this is a week to suppress expectations. Denver finished seventh against the pass at just 187.2 yards allowed per game, and Rice managed only 9.8 PPR points when these teams met last season. RotoBaller calls him a low-end WR2 and specifically points to Patrick Surtain II as the problem. FanDuel lands in almost exactly the same neighborhood with a 12.0 PPR projection and only 68 receiving yards. The volume floor remains real; the ceiling is what Denver threatens. The fade: Downgrade to WR2/FLEX expectations. Start him if that's what the roster requires, but this is a poor week to expect the high-end Rice outcome. Terry McLaurin, WR — Los Bandidos (Bandit) — WAS at PHI McLaurin gets essentially the opposite half of the Jayden Daniels argument. Daniels can escape Philadelphia's pass defense with his legs; McLaurin has to deal with the secondary directly. RotoBaller expects a matchup with Quinyon Mitchell and calls McLaurin risky. FanDuel projects just 49.2 receiving yards, 0.24 touchdowns and 8.2 PPR points against an Eagles defense that finished eighth in passing yards allowed. There is always one-play touchdown upside with McLaurin, but the median outcome looks much more like a FLEX than a comfortable WR2. The fade: FLEX territory. The talent stays in the lineup discussion; the matchup argues strongly against assuming normal production. Stefon Diggs, WR — Dave — WAS at PHI Same Philadelphia problem, different corner. RotoBaller expects Diggs to spend significant time dealing with Cooper DeJean and puts both Washington receivers in its difficult-matchup bucket. The current FantasyPros consensus is even colder: Diggs sits around WR50 for Week 1 and FLEX110 in half-PPR, with an enormous expert range that tells you how little confidence there is in his first game with Washington. The season-long case for Diggs is still defensible—his underlying 2025 efficiency remained good—but this is an awful week to use that long-term argument as a reason to force him into the lineup. The fade: Bench unless lineup depth forces the issue. Between a new offense, target competition and Philadelphia's secondary, Week 1 is better used to learn what his Washington role actually is.
